issues.html_body:
Issue #1 — Thomas Hardy: The Darkling Thrush

AJL14154 Modern Anglophone Poetry | 2026年8月8日

I. Poet Biography — Thomas Hardy (1840-1928)

Thomas Hardy was born on 2 June 1840 in Higher Bockhampton, Dorset, the eldest of four children of Thomas Hardy Sr., a stonemason and builder, and Jemima Hardy (nee Hand). His mother, who had worked in domestic service, encouraged his early education and fostered his reading habits (Millgate, 1982, p. 12).

At sixteen, Hardy was apprenticed to the Dorchester architect John Hicks. In 1862 he moved to London to work for the architect Arthur Blomfield, specializing in church restoration. During this period he began writing poetry, submitting verses to magazines, but met with repeated rejection. He returned to Dorset in 1867 and turned to novel writing as a more viable literary form (Millgate, 2004, p. 34).

Hardy published fourteen novels between 1871 and 1895, including Far from the Madding Crowd (1874), The Return of the Native (1878), The Mayor of Casterbridge (1886), Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891), and Jude the Obscure (1895). The hostile reception of Jude the Obscure — denounced by some critics as immoral and blasphemous — led Hardy to abandon fiction and devote the remaining three decades of his life entirely to poetry (Millgate, 2004, pp. 338-340).

His first poetry collection, Wessex Poems, appeared in 1898. Over the next thirty years he published seven further volumes. "The Darkling Thrush" was written on 31 December 1900 — the final day of the nineteenth century — and first published in The Graphic on 29 December 1900 under the title "By the Century's Deathbed." It was later collected in Poems of the Past and the Present (1901), where Hardy retained the composition date "31 December 1900" (Gibson, 1996, p. 134).

Hardy's first wife, Emma Gifford, whom he married in 1874, died suddenly in November 1912. Her death prompted a remarkable series of elegiac poems, collected in Satires of Circumstance (1914), which many critics regard as his finest poetic achievement (Hynes, 1961, pp. 76-80). Hardy remarried in 1914; his second wife, Florence Dugdale, was thirty-eight years his junior.

Hardy died at Max Gate, his Dorchester home, on 11 January 1928. In a compromise reflecting his own ambivalence about establishment recognition, his body was cremated and interred in Poets' Corner, Westminster Abbey, while his heart was buried in the churchyard at Stinsford, Dorset, alongside the grave of his first wife (Millgate, 2004, pp. 565-567).

Sources: Millgate, M. (1982). Thomas Hardy: A Biography. Oxford UP. | Millgate, M. (2004). Thomas Hardy: A Biography Revisited. Oxford UP. | Gibson, J. (1996). Thomas Hardy: A Literary Life. Palgrave. | Hynes, S. (1961). The Pattern of Hardy's Poetry. U of North Carolina P.

II. The Poem — The Darkling Thrush

Composed 31 December 1900 | First published in The Graphic, 29 December 1900 | Collected in Poems of the Past and the Present (1901)

I leant upon a coppice gate
    When Frost was spectre-grey,
And Winter's dregs made desolate
    The weakening eye of day.
The tangled bine-stems scored the sky
    Like strings of broken lyres,
And all mankind that haunted nigh
    Had sought their household fires.

The land's sharp features seemed to be
    The Century's corpse outleant,
His crypt the cloudy canopy,
    The wind his death-lament.
The ancient pulse of germ and birth
    Was shrunken hard and dry,
And every spirit upon earth
    Seemed fervourless as I.

At once a voice arose among
    The bleak twigs overhead
In a full-hearted evensong
    Of joy illimited;
An aged thrush, frail, gaunt, and small,
    In blast-beruffled plume,
Had chosen thus to fling his soul
    Upon the growing gloom.

So little cause for carolings
    Of such ecstatic sound
Was written on terrestrial things
    Afar or nigh around,
That I could think there trembled through
    His happy good-night air
Some blessed Hope, whereof he knew
    And I was unaware.

Vocabulary Notes

Word Phonetic Definition Example
coppice /ˈkɒpɪs/ 矮林，灌木丛（定期砍伐后再生的小树林） The coppice provided firewood for the village.
spectre /ˈspektə/ 幽灵，幻影 The spectre of war haunted the postwar generation.
dregs /dreɡz/ 残渣，最末尾的部分 He drank the dregs of his coffee and left.
desolate /ˈdesələt/ 荒凉的，凄凉的 The landscape was desolate after the drought.
bine-stems /baɪn stemz/ 藤蔓茎（bine = 攀缘植物的茎） The bine-stems of the honeysuckle twisted round the gate.
lyre /ˈlaɪə/ 里拉琴（古希腊拨弦乐器，象征诗歌与音乐） Apollo was often depicted holding a lyre.
canopy /ˈkænəpi/ 天篷，冠盖；树冠层 The forest canopy blocked out most of the sunlight.
lament /ləˈment/ 挽歌，哀悼；悲痛的表达 The composer wrote a lament for the fallen soldiers.
germ /dʒɜːm/ 胚芽，萌芽；起源（此处指生命的种子） The germ of the idea took root in her undergraduate years.
fervourless /ˈfɜːvələs/ 无热情的，冷漠的（fervour + -less） His fervourless response disappointed the enthusiastic committee.
evensong /ˈiːvənsɒŋ/ 晚祷（英国国教傍晚的祈祷仪式） The choir sang at evensong every Sunday evening.
illimited /ɪlɪmɪtɪd/ 无限的，无边界的（il- + limited） The horizon stretched illimited before the solitary traveller.
blast-beruffled /blɑːst bɪˈrʌfəld/ 被狂风吹乱的（blast + be- + ruffle + -ed） The blast-beruffled flag still hung from the mast.
caroling /ˈkærəlɪŋ/ 唱颂歌，欢唱（carol 的动词形式） The caroling neighbours moved from door to door.
ecstatic /ekˈstætɪk/ 狂喜的，出神的 She was ecstatic upon receiving the acceptance letter.
terrestrial /təˈrestriəl/ 尘世的，地球上的；陆生的 The poem contrasts celestial vision with terrestrial reality.

III. Close Reading Prompts

The following questions adopt a New Critical approach, focusing on textual evidence — imagery, structure, diction, ambiguity, paradox, and irony — rather than biographical or historical context.

1. The hinge of "seemed." The word "seemed" appears in lines 9 and 16 — "The land's sharp features seemed to be / The Century's corpse" and "every spirit upon earth / Seemed fervourless as I." What is the effect of this repeated qualifier? Does it undermine the authority of the speaker's perception, or does it serve another function? Consider how the word operates differently in each instance.

2. Structural symmetries and rupture. The poem divides neatly into two halves: stanzas 1-2 present a landscape of death and stasis; stanzas 3-4 introduce the thrush's song. Yet stanza 3 is the only stanza in which the first-person pronoun "I" does not appear. What is the significance of this absence? How does the formal structure enact the poem's central tension between despair and hope?

3. The paradox of "joy illimited." The thrush sings "a full-hearted evensong / Of joy illimited" in the midst of "the growing gloom." Is this a paradox the poem resolves, sustains, or leaves deliberately ambiguous? Examine how the diction of stanza 3 (e.g., "frail, gaunt, and small" vs. "full-hearted," "illimited") creates tension within a single stanza.

4. "Some blessed Hope, whereof he knew / And I was unaware." The poem ends on a note of epistemological asymmetry: the thrush possesses knowledge the speaker lacks. Is the final line an affirmation of hope, an ironic deflation, or something more complex? Consider the qualifier "Some" (rather than "The" or "A") and the religious resonance of "blessed" in a poem that figures the Century as a corpse.

5. The title: "darkling." "Darkling" means "in the darkness," but it also carries an archaic literary resonance (cf. Milton, Keats). How does the title position the reader before the poem begins? Does the word's phonetic proximity to "darling" introduce an additional layer of ambiguity, or is this an overreading?

6. Personification and the pathetic fallacy. The poem personifies the Century as a corpse with a "crypt" and a "death-lament." How does this personification differ from the treatment of the thrush, which is given a "soul" to "fling"? What does the contrast between these two modes of personification reveal about the poem's hierarchy of being?

IV. Research Frontiers

1. Hahn, H. George. "The Tone in the Tune: An Echo of Burns in Hardy's 'The Darkling Thrush.'" Victorians Institute Journal, vol. 45, no. 1, 2017, pp. 188-194.
DOI: 10.5325/victinstj.45.1.0188
[Open Access] Full text: mdsoar.org
Abstract: Argues that beneath the poem's commonly accepted funereal tone, an echo of Robert Burns's "Auld Lang Syne" may be detected, complicating critical consensus about the poem's mood and suggesting Hardy's musical sensibility introduces a more ambivalent register than previously recognized.

2. Wike, Jonathan. "Toward the 'Coppice Gate': A Reading of Thomas Hardy's 'The Darkling Thrush.'" Philosophy and Literature, vol. 38, no. 1, suppl., 2014, pp. A129-A143.
DOI: 10.1353/phl.2014.0033
[Project MUSE, institutional access]
Summary: Offers a philosophically inflected close reading, examining how the poem stages a threshold experience at the "coppice gate" — a liminal space between century and century, despair and hope, knowing and unknowing.

3. "Surprised by Hope: Possibilities of Spiritual Experience in Victorian Lyric Poetry." Religions, vol. 16, no. 2, 255, 2025.
[Open Access] Full text: mdpi.com
Relevance: Includes a substantial section on "The Darkling Thrush," arguing that the poem explores a nuanced form of agnosticism — not anti-religious, but a recognition of the limits of human knowledge. The thrush's song breaks the speaker's solipsism, and the "blessed Hope" figures not as certainty but as the possibility of meaning beyond the speaker's ken.

4. Abdi, Marwan M. and Hogar N. Abdullah. "Preternatural Landscapes in Hardy's Darkling Thrush and Yushij's It is Night." Academic Journal of Nawroz University, vol. 8, no. 4, 2019.
DOI: 10.25007/ajnu.v8n4a465
[Open Access] Full text: spacefrontiers.org
Abstract: A comparative study examining how Hardy and the Persian modernist poet Nima Yushij use natural landscapes to project speakers' subjective states, suggesting Yushij was influenced by Hardy's symbolist strategies.

5. "Mechanical Birds and Shapes of Ice: Hardy's Vision of the 'Blind Watchmaker.'" Cahiers victoriens et édouardiens, OpenEdition.
[Open Access] Full text: journals.openedition.org
Relevance: Reads "The Darkling Thrush" in dialogue with Darwinian thought, arguing that Hardy's thrush — "no nightingale or skylark, but a mere commonplace bird" — deliberately deflates the Romantic emblem of the inspired songbird, replacing transcendence with biological transience.

issues.subject: 【每日诗歌导读】Issue #2 — W. B. Yeats: The Second Coming
issues.html_body:
Issue #2 — W. B. Yeats: The Second Coming

AJL14154 Modern Anglophone Poetry | 2026年10月11日 | Week: W. B. Yeats (2)

I. Poet Biography — W. B. Yeats (1865-1939)

William Butler Yeats was born on 13 June 1865 in Sandymount, Dublin, the eldest child of the painter John Butler Yeats and Susan Pollexfen, whose family were merchants and shipowners in Sligo. The family moved between London, Dublin and Sligo during his childhood; the Sligo landscape of his mother's family became a lasting source of his imagery (Foster, 1997).

Yeats trained briefly at the Metropolitan School of Art in Dublin before turning to poetry. In 1889 he published The Wanderings of Oisin and Other Poems and met Maud Gonne, the nationalist activist whose repeated refusals of his marriage proposals shaped much of his early love poetry. With Lady Gregory and Edward Martyn he founded the Irish Literary Theatre in 1899, which led to the opening of the Abbey Theatre in 1904 (Foster, 1997).

In October 1917 Yeats married Georgie Hyde-Lees. Days after the wedding she began a practice of "automatic writing", and the material produced over the following years became the basis of his symbolic system A Vision (1925; revised 1937). Its theory of history as a series of interlocking cones or "gyres", each lasting roughly two thousand years, stands behind "The Second Coming" (Foster, 2003).

"The Second Coming" was drafted in January 1919, in the aftermath of the First World War and the Russian Revolution, and while Ireland was moving towards the War of Independence. It first appeared in The Dial and in The Nation (London) in November 1920 and was collected in Michael Robartes and the Dancer (Cuala Press, 1921) (Jeffares, 1968).

Yeats served as a senator of the Irish Free State from 1922 to 1928 and received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923. He died on 28 January 1939 at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin in the south of France; in 1948 his remains were reburied at Drumcliff churchyard, Sligo, under the epitaph from his poem "Under Ben Bulben" (Foster, 2003).

Sources: Foster, R. F. (1997). W. B. Yeats: A Life, I: The Apprentice Mage. Oxford UP. | Foster, R. F. (2003). W. B. Yeats: A Life, II: The Arch-Poet. Oxford UP. | Jeffares, A. N. (1968). A Commentary on the Collected Poems of W. B. Yeats. Stanford UP.

II. The Poem — The Second Coming

Drafted January 1919 | First published in The Dial and The Nation, November 1920 | Collected in Michael Robartes and the Dancer (1921)

Turning and turning in the widening gyre
The falcon cannot hear the falconer;
Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold;
Mere anarchy is loosed upon the world,
The blood-dimmed tide is loosed, and everywhere
The ceremony of innocence is drowned;
The best lack all conviction, while the worst
Are full of passionate intensity.

Surely some revelation is at hand;
Surely the Second Coming is at hand.
The Second Coming! Hardly are those words out
When a vast image out of Spiritus Mundi
Troubles my sight: somewhere in sands of the desert
A shape with lion body and the head of a man,
A gaze blank and pitiless as the sun,
Is moving its slow thighs, while all about it
Reel shadows of the indignant desert birds.
The darkness drops again; but now I know
That twenty centuries of stony sleep
Were vexed to nightmare by a rocking cradle,
And what rough beast, its hour come round at last,
Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born?

Vocabulary Notes

Word Phonetic Definition Example
gyre /ˈdʒaɪə(r)/ 螺旋，旋转（Yeats《A Vision》中表示历史循环的锥形螺旋） The hawk rose in a slow gyre above the valley.
falconer /ˈfɔːlkənə(r)/ 驯鹰人，放鹰者 The falconer whistled, and the bird returned to his glove.
anarchy /ˈænəki/ 无政府状态，混乱 The collapse of the government plunged the province into anarchy.
conviction /kənˈvɪkʃn/ 坚定的信念；定罪 She spoke with quiet conviction about the need for reform.
revelation /ˌrevəˈleɪʃn/ 启示，揭示；（大写）《启示录》 The diary was a revelation of his private doubts.
Spiritus Mundi /ˈspɪrɪtəs ˈmʊndi/ （拉丁语）世界之灵；Yeats 指集体记忆与意象的总库 Yeats imagined Spiritus Mundi as a storehouse of images shared by all minds.
vex /veks/ 使烦恼，搅扰（此处兼有“搅动”之意） The question vexed scholars for a century.
slouch /slaʊtʃ/ 无精打采地走，懒散地垂着身子走 He slouched into the room with his hands in his pockets.

III. Close Reading Prompts

The following questions adopt a New Critical approach, focusing on textual evidence — imagery, structure, diction, ambiguity, paradox, and irony — rather than biographical or historical context.

1. Two kinds of movement. Stanza 1 is dominated by centrifugal motion ("widening gyre", "loosed", "fall apart"), while stanza 2 ends with the slow, heavy motion of the beast ("moving its slow thighs", "Slouches"). How do verbs and rhythm enact these two kinds of movement? Where does the poem's pace change?

2. Passive voice and missing agents. "Mere anarchy is loosed", "The blood-dimmed tide is loosed", "The ceremony of innocence is drowned": who looses, who drowns? What is the effect of withholding the agent in the first stanza, and does the second stanza ever supply one?

3. The broken sonnet. The poem has 22 lines in loose blank verse, with only faint traces of rhyme (e.g. "born" is left unanswered). Read the first stanza as a failed or fractured octave. How does the absence of a stable form relate to the claim that "the centre cannot hold"?

4. Irony in "Second Coming." The title promises the return of Christ, yet the poem delivers a sphinx-like "rough beast". Trace how Christian vocabulary ("revelation", "Bethlehem", "cradle", "twenty centuries") is reused. Is the poem's attitude to the new age horror, fascination, or both?

5. Seeing and knowing. The vision "Troubles my sight", then "The darkness drops again; but now I know". What exactly does the speaker claim to know, and why does the poem end on a question rather than a statement?

IV. Research Frontiers

1. Stallworthy, Jon. Between the Lines: Yeats's Poetry in the Making. Clarendon Press, 1963.
[Monograph, library access]
Relevance: Reconstructs the manuscript drafts of "The Second Coming". The early drafts refer much more explicitly to contemporary political events, and comparing them with the final text shows how Yeats generalised a topical response into apocalyptic myth.

2. Vendler, Helen. Our Secret Discipline: Yeats and Lyric Form. Harvard UP / Oxford UP, 2007.
[Monograph, library access]
Relevance: Reads Yeats's poems through their formal choices (stanza, metre, rhyme). Useful for prompt 3: Vendler treats the form of the poem as part of its argument rather than as decoration.

3. Yeats, W. B. A Vision: The Revised 1937 Edition. Ed. Margaret Mills Harper and Catherine E. Paul. The Collected Works of W. B. Yeats, vol. XIV. Scribner, 2015.
[Primary source, library access]
Relevance: The scholarly edition of the system behind the poem's "gyre" and its two-thousand-year cycle. Read the sections on the historical cones alongside the poem to test how far the poem depends on the system and how far it stands alone.

issues.html_body:
Issue #3 — W. B. Yeats: Sailing to Byzantium

AJL14154 Modern Anglophone Poetry | 2026年10月12日 | Week: W. B. Yeats (2)

I. Poet Biography — Yeats in the 1920s: The Tower

After the Anglo-Irish Treaty of 1921 and the civil war that followed, Yeats became a public figure of the new state: he was appointed to the Senate of the Irish Free State in December 1922 and received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923 (Foster, 2003).

In 1917 he had bought Thoor Ballylee, a Norman tower house near Lady Gregory's estate at Coole Park, Co. Galway, and restored it as a summer home. The tower gave its name to his 1928 collection The Tower, which many critics regard as the peak of his later work (Foster, 2003).

"Sailing to Byzantium" was written in the autumn of 1926, when Yeats was sixty-one. It was first printed in October Blast (Cuala Press, 1927) and placed as the opening poem of The Tower (1928). In a BBC broadcast of 1931 Yeats explained that he was trying to write about "the state of my soul", since it is right for an old man to make his soul, and that Byzantium stood for him as the centre of European civilisation and the source of its spiritual philosophy (Jeffares, 1968).

His interest in Byzantine art went back to a visit to Ravenna in 1907, where he saw the mosaics of San Vitale and Sant'Apollinare Nuovo; the "sages standing in God's holy fire / As in the gold mosaic of a wall" draw on that memory. A second poem, "Byzantium" (1930), returns to the same city (Jeffares, 1968).

Sources: Foster, R. F. (1997). W. B. Yeats: A Life, I: The Apprentice Mage. Oxford UP. | Foster, R. F. (2003). W. B. Yeats: A Life, II: The Arch-Poet. Oxford UP. | Jeffares, A. N. (1968). A Commentary on the Collected Poems of W. B. Yeats. Stanford UP.

II. The Poem — Sailing to Byzantium

Written autumn 1926 | First printed in October Blast (1927) | Opening poem of The Tower (1928)

I
That is no country for old men. The young
In one another's arms, birds in the trees
—Those dying generations—at their song,
The salmon-falls, the mackerel-crowded seas,
Fish, flesh, or fowl, commend all summer long
Whatever is begotten, born, and dies.
Caught in that sensual music all neglect
Monuments of unageing intellect.

II
An aged man is but a paltry thing,
A tattered coat upon a stick, unless
Soul clap its hands and sing, and louder sing
For every tatter in its mortal dress,
Nor is there singing school but studying
Monuments of its own magnificence;
And therefore I have sailed the seas and come
To the holy city of Byzantium.

III
O sages standing in God's holy fire
As in the gold mosaic of a wall,
Come from the holy fire, perne in a gyre,
And be the singing-masters of my soul.
Consume my heart away; sick with desire
And fastened to a dying animal
It knows not what it is; and gather me
Into the artifice of eternity.

IV
Once out of nature I shall never take
My bodily form from any natural thing,
But such a form as Grecian goldsmiths make
Of hammered gold and gold enamelling
To keep a drowsy Emperor awake;
Or set upon a golden bough to sing
To lords and ladies of Byzantium
Of what is past, or passing, or to come.

全诗 32 行，略超 30 行的选段标准；四节 ottava rima 结构不宜拆开，故全文收录。

Vocabulary Notes

Word Phonetic Definition Example
begotten /bɪˈɡɒtn/ （beget 的过去分词）生育，被生出 In the old story, the hero was begotten by a god.
paltry /ˈpɔːltri/ 微不足道的，可怜的 He was offered a paltry sum for years of work.
tatter /ˈtætə(r)/ 碎布条；（复数）破烂衣服 The flag hung in tatters after the storm.
magnificence /mæɡˈnɪfɪsns/ 壮丽，宏伟 Visitors were silenced by the magnificence of the cathedral.
mosaic /məʊˈzeɪɪk/ 马赛克，镶嵌画 The apse is covered with a gold mosaic of the saints.
perne /pɜːn/ （Yeats 自造动词，源自 pern 线轴）螺旋般旋转下降 Yeats asks the sages to perne in a gyre and descend to him.
artifice /ˈɑːtɪfɪs/ 技巧，人工制品；诡计 The garden's natural look was a careful artifice.
enamelling /ɪˈnæmlɪŋ/ 上釉，珐琅工艺 The box was decorated with fine gold enamelling.

III. Close Reading Prompts

The following questions adopt a New Critical approach, focusing on textual evidence — imagery, structure, diction, ambiguity, paradox, and irony — rather than biographical or historical context.

1. "That" and "this." The poem opens with "That is no country", not "This is no country". Where is the speaker standing when he speaks? How does the deictic word establish the journey before the title's "sailing" is ever described?

2. Ambivalent praise of nature. Stanza 1 is meant to reject the natural world, yet its catalogue ("salmon-falls", "mackerel-crowded seas") is among the richest writing in the poem. Does the language undercut the argument? Consider the phrase "Those dying generations".

3. The body as "dying animal." Compare "A tattered coat upon a stick" (stanza 2) with "fastened to a dying animal" (stanza 3). How do these images define the relation between soul and body, and how does each stanza propose to escape it?

4. The golden bird's song. In stanza 4 the speaker wishes to become an artificial bird that sings "Of what is past, or passing, or to come". Compare this line with "Whatever is begotten, born, and dies" in stanza 1. Has the speaker escaped time, or only changed the way he sings about it?

5. Ottava rima. Each stanza follows the ottava rima scheme (abababcc). Look at the closing couplets, e.g. "neglect / intellect" and "me / eternity". How does each couplet resolve, or fail to resolve, the stanza's argument?

IV. Research Frontiers

1. Bradford, Curtis. "Yeats's Byzantium Poems: A Study of Their Development." PMLA, vol. 75, no. 1, 1960, pp. 110-125.
DOI: 10.2307/460433
[Cambridge Core / JSTOR, institutional access]
Summary: A classic manuscript study tracing how "Sailing to Byzantium" and "Byzantium" developed through their drafts. It shows which images Yeats added or removed on the way to the final text and is still the starting point for work on the drafts.

2. Vendler, Helen. Our Secret Discipline: Yeats and Lyric Form. Harvard UP / Oxford UP, 2007.
[Monograph, library access]
Relevance: Contains detailed discussion of Yeats's use of ottava rima, the stanza of "Sailing to Byzantium" and of several other poems in The Tower. Useful for prompt 5.

3. Jeffares, A. Norman. A Commentary on the Collected Poems of W. B. Yeats. Stanford UP, 1968.
[Reference work, library access]
Relevance: Line-by-line notes, including Yeats's own statements about Byzantium and the sources of the mosaic and golden-bird images. A practical companion when preparing for seminar discussion.

issues.html_body:
Issue #4 — Ezra Pound: In a Station of the Metro

AJL14154 Modern Anglophone Poetry | 2026年10月13日 | Week: Ezra Pound

I. Poet Biography — Ezra Pound (1885-1972)

Ezra Loomis Pound was born on 30 October 1885 in Hailey, Idaho, and grew up in Wyncote, near Philadelphia, where his father worked at the U.S. Mint. He studied at the University of Pennsylvania and Hamilton College, then returned to Pennsylvania for graduate work in Romance languages. After a brief teaching post at Wabash College in Indiana ended in 1908, he left for Europe (Moody, 2007).

In Venice in 1908 he published his first book, A Lume Spento, at his own expense, and later that year settled in London. There he became a central organiser of literary modernism: he served as foreign correspondent for Harriet Monroe's Poetry (Chicago), promoted the work of H.D., Richard Aldington, Robert Frost, James Joyce and T. S. Eliot, and spent the winters of 1913-1916 as W. B. Yeats's secretary at Stone Cottage in Sussex (Moody, 2007).

With H.D. and Aldington he launched "Imagisme" in 1912. Its principles were published in Poetry in March 1913: direct treatment of the "thing", no word that does not contribute to the presentation, and composition "in the sequence of the musical phrase", not of the metronome. The anthology Des Imagistes followed in 1914 (Carpenter, 1988).

Pound moved to Paris in 1921 and to Rapallo, Italy, in 1924, where he worked on The Cantos for the rest of his life. His support for Mussolini and his antisemitic wartime broadcasts on Rome Radio led to his arrest by U.S. forces in 1945. Declared unfit to stand trial for treason, he was confined at St Elizabeths Hospital in Washington, D.C., from 1946 to 1958. He returned to Italy and died in Venice on 1 November 1972 (Carpenter, 1988).

"In a Station of the Metro" was first published in Poetry in April 1913, as part of the group "Contemporania", and was collected in Lustra (1916) (Ruthven, 1969).

Sources: Moody, A. D. (2007). Ezra Pound: Poet, Vol. I: The Young Genius 1885–1920. Oxford UP. | Carpenter, H. (1988). A Serious Character: The Life of Ezra Pound. Houghton Mifflin. | Ruthven, K. K. (1969). A Guide to Ezra Pound's Personae (1926). U of California P.

II. The Poem — In a Station of the Metro

First published in Poetry (Chicago), April 1913 | Collected in Lustra (1916)

The apparition of these faces in the crowd;
Petals on a wet, black bough.

以上为通行的 Lustra 版本。1913 年《Poetry》初刊时，Pound 在词组之间留出明显空格，并以冒号连接两行：“The apparition  of these faces  in the crowd  :” 读时可比较两种版式对节奏的影响。

Pound on the poem's origin. In his essay "Vorticism" (The Fortnightly Review, 1 September 1914), Pound recalled stepping out of a train at La Concorde in Paris and seeing "a beautiful face, and then another and another". He first wrote a thirty-line poem and destroyed it as work "of second intensity"; six months later he wrote a poem half that length; a year later he made the two-line version, which he described as a "hokku-like sentence".

Vocabulary Notes

Word Phonetic Definition Example
apparition /ˌæpəˈrɪʃn/ 幽灵，鬼魂；（突然的）出现 The figure in the mist seemed an apparition.
petal /ˈpetl/ 花瓣 Cherry petals drifted onto the pavement.
bough /baʊ/ 大树枝 Snow weighed down the boughs of the pine.
hokku /ˈhɒkuː/ 发句（俳句的旧称） Pound compared his two-line poem to a Japanese hokku.
juxtaposition /ˌdʒʌkstəpəˈzɪʃn/ 并置，并列 The film works through the juxtaposition of war footage and children's songs.
Imagism /ˈɪmɪdʒɪzəm/ 意象派（1910 年代英美诗歌运动） Imagism demanded precise language and the direct treatment of the thing.

III. Close Reading Prompts

The following questions adopt a New Critical approach, focusing on textual evidence — imagery, structure, diction, ambiguity, paradox, and irony — rather than biographical or historical context.

1. A poem without a verb. Neither line has a main verb. What does the poem gain or lose by refusing to say that the faces are, look like or become petals? Is this a metaphor, a simile with its "like" deleted, or something else?

2. The semicolon. The Lustra text joins the two lines with a semicolon; the 1913 text used a colon. How does each mark change the logical relation between "faces" and "Petals"? Which reading do you prefer, and why?

3. "Apparition." The first noun of the poem means both "appearance" and "ghost". Since the setting is underground, does the word introduce a hint of the underworld? How does it colour the brightness of "Petals"?

4. Sound and weight. Count the stressed syllables in line 2: "Petals on a wet, black bough". How do the monosyllables and the comma slow the line down compared with line 1? What does this do to the image?

5. The title as the first line. The title supplies the setting that the poem itself omits. Try reading the poem without its title. How much of the poem's meaning depends on the title, and is that a weakness by Imagist standards?

IV. Research Frontiers

1. Lewis, Pericles. "In a Station of the Metro." The Modernism Lab, Yale University.
[Open Access] Full text: campuspress.yale.edu
Relevance: A short, reliable introduction that reads the poem as a juxtaposition with no verbs and no speaker, links it to Imagist principles and Japanese haiku, and places it in the long European tradition of comparing souls to falling leaves and blossoms.

2. Pound, Ezra. "Vorticism." The Fortnightly Review, 1 September 1914.
[Primary source, widely reprinted]
Relevance: Pound's own account of how the poem was composed and reduced from thirty lines to two, and his theory of the image as "a radiant node or cluster". Essential for comparing the poet's intention with your own close reading.

3. Kenner, Hugh. The Pound Era. U of California P, 1971.
[Monograph, library access]
Relevance: The classic account of Pound's London years. Kenner's discussion of the Metro poem and of the Imagist "image" remains a standard reference point that later criticism argues with.

issues.subject: 【每日诗歌导读】Issue #5 — Ezra Pound: The River-Merchant's Wife: A Letter
issues.html_body:
Issue #5 — Ezra Pound: The River-Merchant's Wife: A Letter

AJL14154 Modern Anglophone Poetry | 2026年10月14日 | Week: Ezra Pound

I. Poet Biography — Pound and Cathay (1915)

In late 1913 Mary McNeil Fenollosa, widow of the American orientalist Ernest Fenollosa (1853-1908), gave Pound her husband's notebooks. They contained word-by-word glosses of classical Chinese poems that Fenollosa had studied in Japan with Japanese scholars, and therefore gave the poets' names in their Japanese readings: Li Bai (Li Po) appears as "Rihaku" (Moody, 2007).

Pound, who did not read Chinese at the time, worked from these glosses to produce Cathay, a small book of fourteen poems published by Elkin Mathews in April 1915. Its poems of exile, separation and frontier war were read in Britain against the background of the First World War (Moody, 2007).

"The River-Merchant's Wife: A Letter" is Pound's version of Li Bai's 《长干行》 ("Chang Gan Xing"). Pound's title adds the words "A Letter", which do not appear in the original (Ruthven, 1969).

In his introduction to Pound's Selected Poems (1928), T. S. Eliot described Pound as "the inventor of Chinese poetry for our time", a phrase that has framed debates about Cathay ever since: is it translation, adaptation, or original modernist poetry? (Carpenter, 1988).

Sources: Moody, A. D. (2007). Ezra Pound: Poet, Vol. I: The Young Genius 1885–1920. Oxford UP. | Carpenter, H. (1988). A Serious Character: The Life of Ezra Pound. Houghton Mifflin. | Ruthven, K. K. (1969). A Guide to Ezra Pound's Personae (1926). U of California P.

II. The Poem — The River-Merchant's Wife: A Letter

From Cathay (Elkin Mathews, April 1915) | After Li Bai 李白《长干行》

While my hair was still cut straight across my forehead
I played about the front gate, pulling flowers.
You came by on bamboo stilts, playing horse,
You walked about my seat, playing with blue plums.
And we went on living in the village of Chokan:
Two small people, without dislike or suspicion.

At fourteen I married My Lord you.
I never laughed, being bashful.
Lowering my head, I looked at the wall.
Called to, a thousand times, I never looked back.

At fifteen I stopped scowling,
I desired my dust to be mingled with yours
Forever and forever and forever.
Why should I climb the look out?

At sixteen you departed,
You went into far Ku-to-yen, by the river of swirling eddies,
And you have been gone five months.
The monkeys make sorrowful noise overhead.

You dragged your feet when you went out.
By the gate now, the moss is grown, the different mosses,
Too deep to clear them away!
The leaves fall early this autumn, in wind.
The paired butterflies are already yellow with August
Over the grass in the West garden;
They hurt me. I grow older.
If you are coming down through the narrows of the river Kiang,
Please let me know beforehand,
And I will come out to meet you
                    As far as Cho-fu-Sa.

                                        By Rihaku

原诗对照：李白《长干行》（其一）

妾发初覆额，折花门前剧。郎骑竹马来，绕床弄青梅。
同居长干里，两小无嫌猜。十四为君妇，羞颜未尝开。
低头向暗壁，千唤不一回。十五始展眉，愿同尘与灰。
常存抱柱信，岂上望夫台。十六君远行，瞿塘滟滪堆。
五月不可触，猿声天上哀。门前迟行迹，一一生绿苔。
苔深不能扫，落叶秋风早。八月蝴蝶黄，双飞西园草。
感此伤妾心，坐愁红颜老。早晚下三巴，预将书报家。
相迎不道远，直至长风沙。

Vocabulary Notes

Word Phonetic Definition Example
stilts /stɪlts/ 高跷；（此处 bamboo stilts 对应原诗“竹马”） Children raced each other on wooden stilts.
bashful /ˈbæʃfl/ 害羞的，腼腆的 The bashful boy hid behind his mother.
scowl /skaʊl/ 皱眉，怒视（对应原诗“展眉”的反面） She scowled at the noise from the street.
mingle /ˈmɪŋɡl/ 混合，交融 The smell of rain mingled with the scent of pine.
eddy /ˈedi/ 漩涡，涡流 Leaves spun in the eddies below the bridge.
narrows /ˈnærəʊz/ （河、海的）狭窄处，峡口 The boat slowed as it entered the narrows.

III. Close Reading Prompts

The following questions adopt a New Critical approach, focusing on textual evidence — imagery, structure, diction, ambiguity, paradox, and irony — rather than biographical or historical context.

1. Original and version side by side. Read Pound's text against Li Bai's 《长干行》 below. Pound omits the allusion 「常存抱柱信」 (the story of Wei Sheng, who drowned rather than break a promise) and keeps only "Why should I climb the look out?" for 「岂上望夫台」. What happens to the wife's voice when the allusions disappear?

2. "Five months." Li Bai's 「五月不可触」 refers to the fifth month, when the Qutang Gorge (瞿塘峡, Yanyu Rock 滟滪堆) is dangerous to pass. Pound's gloss gave "five months", so the line now measures how long the husband has been away. Is this an error that the poem turns into a new meaning?

3. Syntax as character. "At fourteen I married My Lord you." The odd word order imitates a gloss rather than idiomatic English. How do such slightly foreign constructions create the speaker's voice: shy, formal, intimate?

4. Time and structure. The poem moves through ages (fourteen, fifteen, sixteen) and then into seasons. How does the last verse paragraph abandon this neat chronology, and where does the emotion break through ("They hurt me. I grow older.")?

5. Restraint. The speaker never names her feelings directly until the end. Find the images that carry emotion instead (the moss, the paired butterflies). How does this practice relate to the Imagist rule of "direct treatment of the thing"?

IV. Research Frontiers

1. Cîndea, Iulia Elena, and Diana Ștefania Jerpel. "Not New Poems but Translations: Ezra Pound's Image-Centered Cathay from Chinese Tang Poetry." Humanities, vol. 14, no. 12, article 229, 2025.
DOI: 10.3390/h14120229
[Open Access] Full text: mdpi.com
Summary: Argues that Cathay should be read as translation of Tang poetry rather than independent modernist verse, and that it stays faithful chiefly by keeping and intensifying visual detail while losing sound patterns and cultural specifics. Includes a close comparison of two Li Bai poems; a good model for your own comparison in prompts 1-2.

2. Yip, Wai-lim. Ezra Pound's Cathay. Princeton UP, 1969.
[Monograph, library access]
Relevance: The classic study by a bilingual poet-scholar, comparing each Cathay poem with its Chinese original and the Fenollosa notes. It argues that Pound often captured the poetic mode of the originals despite errors of detail.

3. Qian, Zhaoming. Orientalism and Modernism: The Legacy of China in Pound and Williams. Duke UP, 1995.
[Monograph, library access]
Relevance: Examines how Chinese poetry and art shaped Pound's (and William Carlos Williams's) modernism, with close attention to Cathay and its sources.

issues.subject: 【每日诗歌导读】Issue #6 — Ezra Pound: The Return
issues.html_body:
Issue #6 — Ezra Pound: The Return

AJL14154 Modern Anglophone Poetry | 2026年10月15日 | Week: Ezra Pound

I. Poet Biography — Pound in London: Ripostes (1912)

Pound's first London years were spent absorbing and imitating older models: Provençal troubadours, Dante, Browning's dramatic monologue and the poets of the 1890s. Collections such as Personae (1909) and Exultations (1909) show this apprenticeship (Moody, 2007).

Ripostes, published by Stephen Swift in October 1912, marks a turning point. It contains his version of the Anglo-Saxon "The Seafarer" and, as an appendix, the poems of his friend T. E. Hulme, introduced with the first printed use of the word "Imagistes" (Moody, 2007).

"The Return" first appeared in The English Review in June 1912 and was collected in Ripostes. Its free, irregular lines, set at varying indents, are an early example of Pound's search for a rhythm based on "the musical phrase" rather than regular metre (Ruthven, 1969).

Sources: Moody, A. D. (2007). Ezra Pound: Poet, Vol. I: The Young Genius 1885–1920. Oxford UP. | Carpenter, H. (1988). A Serious Character: The Life of Ezra Pound. Houghton Mifflin. | Ruthven, K. K. (1969). A Guide to Ezra Pound's Personae (1926). U of California P.

II. The Poem — The Return

First published in The English Review, June 1912 | Collected in Ripostes (1912)

See, they return; ah, see the tentative
Movements, and the slow feet,
The trouble in the pace and the uncertain
Wavering!

See, they return, one, and by one,
With fear, as half-awakened;
As if the snow should hesitate
And murmur in the wind,
          and half turn back;
These were the "Wing'd-with-Awe,"
          Inviolable.

Gods of the wingèd shoe!
With them the silver hounds,
          sniffing the trace of air!

Haie! Haie!
          These were the swift to harry;
These the keen-scented;
These were the souls of blood.

Slow on the leash,
          pallid the leash-men!

Vocabulary Notes

Word Phonetic Definition Example
tentative /ˈtentətɪv/ 试探性的，犹豫不决的 The child took a few tentative steps across the ice.
waver /ˈweɪvə(r)/ 摇摆，踌躇；（光、声）颤动 Her voice wavered as she read the letter.
inviolable /ɪnˈvaɪələbl/ 不可侵犯的，神圣的 They treated the right of asylum as inviolable.
harry /ˈhæri/ 袭扰，追逐，不断侵扰 Wolves harried the herd through the winter.
keen-scented /kiːn ˈsentɪd/ 嗅觉敏锐的 The keen-scented dogs found the trail at once.
pallid /ˈpælɪd/ 苍白的，无生气的 His pallid face showed weeks of illness.
leash /liːʃ/ （牵狗的）皮带 Dogs must be kept on a leash in the park.

III. Close Reading Prompts

The following questions adopt a New Critical approach, focusing on textual evidence — imagery, structure, diction, ambiguity, paradox, and irony — rather than biographical or historical context.

1. Who are "they"? The poem never names its subject. Gods, hunters, hounds? Collect the clues ("Wing'd-with-Awe", "wingèd shoe", "silver hounds", "souls of blood"). Why might Pound keep the identity open?

2. Lineation as gesture. Lines are broken and indented irregularly, e.g. "Wavering!" alone on a line, or "and half turn back;" set off to the right. Read the poem aloud. How does the layout make you hesitate in the same way that the returning figures hesitate?

3. Past against present. The poem moves between present tense ("they return") and past tense ("These were the swift to harry"). What contrast is drawn between what these figures were and what they are now?

4. The simile of the snow. "As if the snow should hesitate / And murmur in the wind". Why snow? Consider its quietness, its drifting motion, and the way it melts. How does this one simile set the tone of the whole poem?

5. The ending. "Slow on the leash, / pallid the leash-men!" The poem ends not with the gods but with their keepers. What is suggested by the shift to the "leash-men" and their pallor? Is the return a revival or a ghostly procession?

IV. Research Frontiers

1. Witemeyer, Hugh. The Poetry of Ezra Pound: Forms and Renewal, 1908–1920. U of California P, 1969.
[Monograph, library access]
Relevance: Traces Pound's early development from the 1890s manner to Imagism, with attention to the poems of Ripostes. Helpful for placing "The Return" between the older and the newer Pound.

2. Moody, A. David. Ezra Pound: Poet. A Portrait of the Man and His Work, Vol. I: The Young Genius 1885-1920. Oxford UP, 2007.
[Monograph, library access]
Relevance: The standard critical biography, which reads the poems in close relation to Pound's life in London. Its chapters on 1911-1912 cover Ripostes and the emergence of Imagism.

3. Kenner, Hugh. The Pound Era. U of California P, 1971.
[Monograph, library access]
Relevance: Kenner's account of Pound's metrical experiments is a classic reference for discussing how the free verse of "The Return" differs from regular metre.

issues.subject: 【每日诗歌导读】Issue #7 — Ezra Pound: A Pact
issues.html_body:
Issue #7 — Ezra Pound: A Pact

AJL14154 Modern Anglophone Poetry | 2026年10月16日 | Week: Ezra Pound

I. Poet Biography — Pound and Whitman

Pound's relation to Walt Whitman (1819-1892) was ambivalent from the start. In a short prose piece dated 1909 and titled "What I Feel About Walt Whitman", he wrote that Whitman "is America" and admitted that he read him "(in many places) with acute pain", while recognising how much he owed him. The essay was not published until 1955 (Ruthven, 1969).

"A Pact" was first published in Poetry in April 1913, in the same "Contemporania" group as "In a Station of the Metro", and later collected in Lustra (1916) (Ruthven, 1969).

For an American poet living in London, Whitman represented both the possibility of a distinctively American free verse and a looseness of form that the Imagists wanted to discipline. "A Pact" stages this negotiation in nine lines (Moody, 2007).

Sources: Moody, A. D. (2007). Ezra Pound: Poet, Vol. I: The Young Genius 1885–1920. Oxford UP. | Carpenter, H. (1988). A Serious Character: The Life of Ezra Pound. Houghton Mifflin. | Ruthven, K. K. (1969). A Guide to Ezra Pound's Personae (1926). U of California P.

II. The Poem — A Pact

First published in Poetry (Chicago), April 1913 | Collected in Lustra (1916)

I make a pact with you, Walt Whitman—
I have detested you long enough.
I come to you as a grown child
Who has had a pig-headed father;
I am old enough now to make friends.
It was you that broke the new wood,
Now is a time for carving.
We have one sap and one root—
Let there be commerce between us.

Vocabulary Notes

Word Phonetic Definition Example
pact /pækt/ 协定，契约 The two countries signed a non-aggression pact.
detest /dɪˈtest/ 憎恶，厌恶 She detested being interrupted.
pig-headed /ˌpɪɡ ˈhedɪd/ 固执的，顽固的 He was too pig-headed to admit his mistake.
sap /sæp/ 树液；元气 Sap rises in the trees in spring.
commerce /ˈkɒmɜːs/ 商业，贸易；（旧）交往，交流 The port grew rich on commerce with the East.

III. Close Reading Prompts

The following questions adopt a New Critical approach, focusing on textual evidence — imagery, structure, diction, ambiguity, paradox, and irony — rather than biographical or historical context.

1. From "detested" to "commerce." Trace the emotional movement of the poem line by line. Where exactly does hostility turn into reconciliation? Is the reconciliation complete?

2. The family metaphor. Pound casts himself as "a grown child" and Whitman as "a pig-headed father". What does this metaphor concede to Whitman, and what does it claim for Pound?

3. Wood and carving. "It was you that broke the new wood, / Now is a time for carving." What two kinds of work are being distinguished? How might this describe the relation between Whitman's free verse and Imagism?

4. "Commerce." The last word can mean trade, exchange or intercourse. Why choose an economic word to end a poem about poetic inheritance? Does it sound generous, wary, or ironic?

5. Form against content. The poem itself is in short, controlled free-verse lines, unlike Whitman's long catalogues. In what sense does the form of "A Pact" carry out the "carving" that the poem describes?

IV. Research Frontiers

1. Pound, Ezra. "What I Feel About Walt Whitman" (1909). First published in American Literature, vol. 27, no. 1, 1955, ed. Herbert Bergman.
[Primary source; JSTOR, institutional access]
Relevance: Pound's early, candid statement on Whitman, written four years before "A Pact". Read together with the poem to see how the prose ambivalence was condensed into nine lines.

2. Witemeyer, Hugh. The Poetry of Ezra Pound: Forms and Renewal, 1908–1920. U of California P, 1969.
[Monograph, library access]
Relevance: Discusses Pound's early models and his attempt to forge an American idiom in London, including the place of Whitman in that project.

3. Ruthven, K. K. A Guide to Ezra Pound's Personae (1926). U of California P, 1969.
[Reference work, library access]
Relevance: Gives first-publication details and annotations for each poem in Personae, including "A Pact". A reliable first stop for dates and allusions.

issues.subject: 【每日诗歌导读】Issue #8 — Ezra Pound: Hugh Selwyn Mauberley (V)
issues.html_body:
Issue #8 — Ezra Pound: Hugh Selwyn Mauberley (V)

AJL14154 Modern Anglophone Poetry | 2026年10月17日 | Week: Ezra Pound

I. Poet Biography — Leaving London: Hugh Selwyn Mauberley (1920)

By 1920 Pound had become disillusioned with literary London, and the First World War had killed several of his friends, among them the sculptor Henri Gaudier-Brzeska, who died in action in France in June 1915 and to whom Pound had devoted a memoir (1916) (Moody, 2007).

Hugh Selwyn Mauberley was published by John Rodker's Ovid Press in June 1920, shortly before Pound left London for Paris. It is a sequence of eighteen short poems in two parts, presenting the career of an imaginary aesthete-poet and, through him, a satirical picture of English literary culture (Moody, 2007).

Section V belongs to the first part, "E. P. Ode pour l'élection de son sépulchre". Sections IV and V together form Pound's most direct response to the war. Pound later told readers not to identify him simply with Mauberley, a point critics still debate (Ruthven, 1969).

Sources: Moody, A. D. (2007). Ezra Pound: Poet, Vol. I: The Young Genius 1885–1920. Oxford UP. | Carpenter, H. (1988). A Serious Character: The Life of Ezra Pound. Houghton Mifflin. | Ruthven, K. K. (1969). A Guide to Ezra Pound's Personae (1926). U of California P.

II. The Poem — Hugh Selwyn Mauberley, Section V

From Hugh Selwyn Mauberley (Ovid Press, June 1920) | Part I: "E. P. Ode pour l'élection de son sépulchre"

There died a myriad,
And of the best, among them,
For an old bitch gone in the teeth,
For a botched civilization,

Charm, smiling at the good mouth,
Quick eyes gone under earth's lid,

For two gross of broken statues,
For a few thousand battered books.

整组诗共 18 首，此处选第一部分第 V 首，建议课后连同第 IV 首（"These fought in any case"）一起读。

Vocabulary Notes

Word Phonetic Definition Example
myriad /ˈmɪriəd/ 无数，极大数量 A myriad of stars filled the desert sky.
botched /bɒtʃt/ 搞糟的，拙劣的 The botched repair left the roof leaking.
gross /ɡrəʊs/ （量词）罗，十二打（144 个）；粗俗的 The shop ordered two gross of pencils.
battered /ˈbætəd/ 破旧的，磨损的 He still carried his battered old suitcase.
sepulchre /ˈseplkə(r)/ 坟墓，墓穴（标题中 sépulchre 为法语） The knight was laid in a stone sepulchre.

III. Close Reading Prompts

The following questions adopt a New Critical approach, focusing on textual evidence — imagery, structure, diction, ambiguity, paradox, and irony — rather than biographical or historical context.

1. The bathos of "For." The repeated "For" introduces what the dead died for: "an old bitch gone in the teeth", "a botched civilization", "broken statues", "battered books". How does each item lower the value of the cause? What tone results?

2. "Two gross" and "a few thousand." Why does Pound use the language of quantity and trade (a "gross" is a dozen dozen) for works of art? Compare this with the uncountable "myriad" of the dead in line 1.

3. The middle couplet. "Charm, smiling at the good mouth, / Quick eyes gone under earth's lid". This is the only passage that describes the dead as individuals. How does its imagery differ from the rest of the poem, and what is the effect of its placement at the centre?

4. "Earth's lid." Analyse the metaphor of the earth as a "lid". What does it combine (eyelid, coffin lid)? How does the word "Quick" (alive, swift) work against it?

5. Satire and elegy. Is this poem a satire of the civilization that sent men to die, an elegy for the dead, or both at once? Point to the words that pull in each direction.

IV. Research Frontiers

1. Espey, John J. Ezra Pound's Mauberley: A Study in Composition. U of California P, 1955.
[Monograph, library access]
Relevance: The first book-length study of the sequence, examining its sources and composition and the vexed question of how far Mauberley is a mask for Pound himself.

2. Ruthven, K. K. A Guide to Ezra Pound's Personae (1926). U of California P, 1969.
[Reference work, library access]
Relevance: Annotates the allusions throughout Mauberley, including the French and classical references in the title of Part I. Useful before reading the whole sequence.

3. Kenner, Hugh. The Pound Era. U of California P, 1971.
[Monograph, library access]
Relevance: Kenner's chapters on Pound's London period include a reading of Mauberley as a farewell to London and to an earlier version of the poet himself.
